images.title: One job at a time
images.alt: Five-stage writing process: decide the one question, outline from reader questions, write the answer first, draft without editing, edit in passes.
images.caption: Doing these jobs in order stops each one from interrupting the other two.

items.label: Decide the question
items.text: One sentence: this article answers [question] for [reader].

items.label: Outline
items.text: The reader's questions, in order, become your headings.

items.label: Answer first
items.text: The two-or-three-sentence answer becomes the opening.

items.label: Draft without editing
items.text: Leave it rough. Type TK for missing facts and keep moving.

items.label: Edit in passes
items.text: Cut, check facts, then read it aloud.

images.title: Three edits, one job each
images.alt: Three editing passes: cut warm-ups and repeats, check every fact and TK against its source, then read the draft aloud and proofread.
images.caption: One read-through that tries to catch everything catches very little.

items.title: Cut
items.text: Delete warm-ups, repeats and sentences the reader wouldn't miss.

items.title: Check facts
items.text: Open the source for every fact and TK. If you can't confirm a number, remove it.

items.title: Read it aloud
items.text: Fix sentences that run long or sound unnatural, then proofread.

images.after: Where AI drafting helps, and where it doesn't
images.title: Where AI drafting fits
images.alt: Comparison of where AI tools help with writing, such as outlines and rough drafts, and where they fall short, such as invented facts and padded prose.
images.caption: An AI draft still needs all three editing passes, with extra care on the fact check.
